items.prompt: A user requests "add a CSV export button." What's the key risk of building exactly that, without further investigation?
choices: CSV export is technically difficult to implement correctly
The request already encodes the requester's own assumed solution — building it literally means inheriting whatever unvalidated problem statement they had in mind, without confirming it's the best fit
Users never actually use export features once built
There is no risk; taking feature requests literally is always correct
items.explanation: A request phrased as a solution smuggles in an implicit, unvalidated problem statement. The risk isn't that CSV export is hard to build — it's that it might not actually be the best (or even a good) fit for the real underlying need, which was never separately checked.
items.reference:
Requested

"Add a CSV export button"

Actually needed

Early warning when a metric trends the wrong way

Why: a request names one guess at a solution, not the problem itself — building it literally skips checking whether that guess was even a good fit.
items.learnMore:
Why a feature request isn't a problem statement

A request like "add a CSV export button" reads as concrete and actionable, which makes it tempting to build directly. But it already names a mechanism (CSV export), not the underlying need that mechanism is meant to serve. Building it literally means silently adopting the requester's first guess at a solution as if it were a validated specification.

The fix isn't to distrust every request — it's to treat it as a clue pointing at a real problem, and to check what that problem actually is before committing implementation time to the requester's specific proposed fix.

Common mistake

Assuming a request is trustworthy because it's specific and easy to build. Specificity and correctness are unrelated — a very specific request can still be the wrong fix.

items.prompt: What does the "five whys" technique do, as described in this unit?
choices: It forces a requester to justify their request to a manager five separate times
It repeatedly asks "why do you need that?" to push past a stated request toward the actual underlying need it's meant to serve
It requires exactly five different people to approve a feature before it's built
It's a way to reject any request that can't be justified in under five sentences
items.explanation: The five whys is a repeated-questioning technique, not an approval process — its purpose is to keep peeling back layers of "solution" until what's left is an actual need, not another proposed fix.
items.reference:
"I want a CSV export"
why? → "So I can build a report"
why? → "So I can see weekly trends"
why? → "So I know if it's getting worse"
Root need: early visibility into a worsening trend
items.learnMore:
What each "why" is actually testing

Each "why" answer should be checked against one question: does this still describe a solution, or does it finally describe a need? "So I can build a report" is still a solution (a report is a chosen artifact, not a need). "So I know if it's getting worse before it's a crisis" is a need — it doesn't presuppose any particular tool or format.

Once an answer is genuinely need-shaped, the technique is done — pushing further tends to over-abstract into something too generic to build against.

Common mistake

Stopping at the first "why" answer and treating it as the root need, even when it's still solution-shaped (like "a report").

items.prompt: In the chain "I want a CSV export" → ... → "early visibility into a worsening trend," what does the final answer represent that the first one didn't?
choices: A more detailed technical specification of the same CSV export feature
A need stated without reference to any particular tool or format, which can be evaluated against multiple different candidate solutions
A complaint about the CSV export idea being a bad one
Nothing — both statements describe exactly the same thing in different words
items.explanation: "CSV export" names one specific mechanism. "Early visibility into a worsening trend" names the underlying need with no mechanism attached — which is what makes it possible to compare CSV export against a live chart or an alert threshold on equal footing.

items.prompt: What does the "jobs to be done" framing mean when it says users don't want a product, they "hire" it?
choices: Users pay a subscription fee, which is compared metaphorically to hiring an employee
Users bring a specific job they need done in a specific context, and evaluate whether a given product makes progress on that job — the product is a means, not the goal itself
Companies should literally interview users before letting them use a product
Jobs to be done only applies to enterprise software with formal procurement
items.explanation: The "hiring" metaphor is about the product being a means to an end, not the end itself — the user's actual goal is progress on a job, and the product is judged by how well it advances that job in the user's specific context.
items.reference:
Feature-request framing

"They want a CSV export"

Jobs-to-be-done framing

"They're hiring something to help them notice a worsening trend"

Why: the job framing evaluates fit against the underlying goal, not just whether the requested feature exists.
items.learnMore:
Why "hiring" is a useful metaphor

Thinking of a product as being "hired" for a job reframes the evaluation question. Instead of "does it have the feature that was requested," the question becomes "does it make real progress on the job the user actually has" — which opens the door to solutions the user never explicitly asked for, because they only know the tools they've already tried.

This is the same shift the five whys produces from a different angle: both techniques exist to get past the literal request and find the actual thing being accomplished.

Common mistake

Treating "jobs to be done" as just a rebranding of "user needs" with no practical difference — the job framing specifically forces context (when, how often, how high-stakes) into the picture, which a bare "need" statement can leave out.

items.prompt: Why does understanding the "job" behind a request matter more than understanding the literal feature request itself?
choices: It doesn't — the literal feature request is always the more useful thing to understand
Understanding the job lets you evaluate whether a different, better solution could serve the same underlying need — something you can't do if you only understand the requested feature
Understanding the job is only useful for marketing copy, not for engineering decisions
The job and the feature request are always identical, so there's no practical difference
items.explanation: Knowing the job opens up comparison across candidate solutions; knowing only the feature request locks you into evaluating just that one option, since you have no independent way to judge whether it's actually the best fit.

items.prompt: Which of these passes the "one-sentence problem statement" test (states the problem with zero reference to the proposed solution)?
choices: "Users need a CSV export so they can track trends"
"Users need to notice when a metric is trending in the wrong direction, in time to act, without a manual weekly ritual"
"Users want a dark mode toggle"
"We should add bulk delete for tickets"
items.explanation: The first, third, and fourth options each bake a specific solution into the problem statement itself, which forecloses comparing alternatives. Only the second describes the underlying need without naming how it should be solved.
items.reference:
StatementPasses?
"Users need a CSV export so they can track trends"No
"Users need to notice a worsening trend in time to act"Yes

Why: the passing statement names no tool, format, or mechanism — only the underlying need.
items.learnMore:
Why zero solution reference is the actual test

The one-sentence test isn't about brevity or clarity in general — it's specifically about whether the sentence names a mechanism. "Users need a CSV export so they can track trends" is clear and short, but it still fails, because "CSV export" is baked in as if it were part of the problem rather than one candidate answer to it.

A passing statement can be evaluated against several different candidate solutions side by side; a failing one has already picked the winner before the comparison even starts.

Common mistake

Assuming a statement passes just because it's phrased as a full sentence with a "so that" clause — the solution can still be hiding inside the "so that" part, as in the failing example.

items.prompt: This unit says a feature request should be treated as a "clue," not the final specification. What does that mean in practice?
choices: Feature requests should be ignored entirely and replaced with what the team thinks is best
A request is useful evidence about what the underlying problem might be, but it needs to be validated before being treated as the actual thing to build
Only requests from senior stakeholders count as real clues
"Clue" means the request is probably wrong and should be treated with suspicion by default
items.explanation: Treating a request as a clue means taking it seriously as a starting point for investigation, not dismissing it — but also not accepting it as the final word on what to build without checking the problem underneath it.
items.reference:
🎫 Request: evidence about a problem, not the problem itself
🔍 Investigate: what need is this request pointing at?
✅ Validate before building: is the requested solution actually the best fit?
items.learnMore:
Clue, not verdict

This unit is explicit that the point isn't to ignore what users ask for — a request is real evidence that something is bothering someone, and that's worth taking seriously. The shift is in what you do with that evidence: instead of building it as-is, you use it as a starting point to find the actual problem, and only then decide what to build.

This is a middle path between two extremes: blindly building every literal request, and dismissing requests as unreliable and building whatever the team prefers instead. Both extremes skip the actual validation step.

Common mistake

Reading "treat requests as clues" as license to override what users ask for based on the team's own assumptions, without ever actually talking to them.

items.prompt: Which of these best reflects the balance this unit strikes between "take user requests seriously" and "don't just build them literally"?
choices: Ignore all feature requests and rely entirely on internal judgment about what users need
Investigate the problem behind every request before building, while still treating the request itself as real, useful evidence of a genuine problem worth solving
Build every request exactly as written, since users know their own needs better than anyone else
Only investigate requests that come from paying customers
items.explanation: The unit explicitly rejects both extremes — it's not about distrust of users, and it's not about literal compliance either. The request is respected as a signal; the underlying problem still has to be checked before committing to a build.

items.prompt: "I want a CSV export so I can build a report." Is this a good stopping point for the five-whys process?
choices: Yes — "so I can build a report" is clearly a root need
No — "a report" is itself still a solution-shaped answer, not a root need; the technique's value comes from pushing past the first plausible-sounding answer
Yes, because any answer after the first "why" counts as sufficient
No, because five whys always requires exactly five iterations, no more, no less
items.explanation: Stopping at the first answer and calling it the root need is one of the unit's explicit failure modes — a report is a chosen solution too, just one step removed from CSV export. The technique needs to be pushed until the answer is genuinely a need, not another solution wearing different clothes.
items.reference:
Depth 1: "a report" — still a solution
Depth 2: "see weekly trends" — closer, still a bit solution-shaped
Depth 3: "know before it's a crisis" — a genuine need

Why: not every "why" answer counts as done — the answer has to stop naming an artifact and start naming a reason.
items.learnMore:
Why stopping too early defeats the technique

The five whys only does its job if each answer is checked against the same test used for the original request: does this still name a solution, or does it finally name a need? "A report" fails that test just as much as "a CSV export" does — it's a chosen artifact, not a reason.

Stopping at the first plausible-sounding answer is a common shortcut precisely because it feels like progress was made. The unit's guidance is to keep checking each answer against the same standard, not to stop as soon as the answer sounds a bit more specific.

Common mistake

Treating any deeper-sounding answer as automatically the root need, without checking whether it's still solution-shaped.

items.explanation: The unit warns that pushing too far turns a specific, actionable need into something so abstract it no longer helps distinguish between candidate solutions — the goal is a usable need statement, not maximum abstraction.

items.prompt: According to the unit's "usefulness for choosing a build" chart, why isn't usefulness highest right at depth 0 (the literal ask)?
choices: Because depth 0 is somehow less specific than deeper answers
Because depth 0 has already committed to one particular solution, which makes it useless for comparing alternatives, even though it's fully specific
Because usefulness always increases in a straight line with depth, with no exceptions
Because the literal ask is always factually wrong
items.explanation: Depth 0 is maximally specific but has already picked a solution — it can't be used to evaluate whether that solution is actually the best fit, since there's no independent need statement left to compare it against.
items.reference:

0
2
3-4

Why: usefulness peaks in the middle — too shallow is solution-locked, too deep is over-abstracted.
items.learnMore:
Reading the peak-then-fall shape

The chart isn't claiming "deeper is always better" — it's claiming there's a sweet spot. Too shallow (depth 0-1) and the statement is still tied to one specific mechanism, which forecloses comparison. Too deep (5+) and the statement becomes so generic ("I need to feel secure") that it no longer helps distinguish between candidate solutions either.

The useful zone is where the statement names a real need with no particular mechanism attached, but is still specific enough to point at a bounded set of realistic solutions.

Common mistake

Assuming "ask more whys" is always the safe default. Past a point, more whys actively makes the problem statement less useful, not more.

Usefulness never falls — it keeps climbing indefinitely with more whys
items.explanation: Past the sweet spot, additional whys keep abstracting the need until it stops pointing at a specific, actionable problem — which is just as useless for choosing a build as being locked into one solution at depth 0.

items.prompt: Two users both ask for "a way to see this metric over time." One needs it for a quick weekly glance; the other needs it for a one-off deep investigation. Per the "jobs to be done" framing, why does this context matter?
choices: It doesn't — the same feature (a chart) always serves both cases equally well

The same underlying need calls for different solutions depending on context — a lightweight recurring glance and a deep one-time analysis are different jobs, even though both are nominally "see this metric over time"
Context only matters for enterprise customers, not general users
Jobs to be done applies only to entirely new products, not existing features
items.explanation: Jobs to be done frames a need as tied to a specific context, not just an abstract description. A generic CSV export serves a deep one-off investigation reasonably well but poorly serves a routine quick glance — the same words ("see trends") hide two different jobs with different best-fit solutions.
items.reference:
JobBest-fit solution
Weekly glance (routine, low-stakes)A live trend line already on the dashboard
One-off deep investigationA raw data export to slice freely

Why: the same words ("see this over time") hide two different jobs — context, not wording, determines the best-fit solution.
items.learnMore:
Why context has to be part of the need statement

A need statement that leaves out context ("see this metric over time") is ambiguous between two very different jobs with opposite best-fit solutions. A live chart is fast and instant, ideal for a routine glance, but poor for open-ended slicing. A raw export is the reverse — flexible for deep analysis, but too much friction for a five-second check.

Jobs to be done forces the context (how often, how high-stakes, what happens next) into the need statement precisely because leaving it out makes two genuinely different problems look identical on paper.

Common mistake

Building one general-purpose solution and assuming it serves "the need" for everyone, without checking whether the context differs across requesters.

items.explanation: The mismatch isn't about the data being wrong — it's about friction versus context. A multi-step manual export workflow is a bad fit for something that needs to happen quickly, routinely, with minimal effort, even if it technically produces the right numbers.

It's easy to misuse the five whys as a rhetorical tool for pushing back on requests — "well, why do you REALLY need that?" used to erode a request rather than understand it. Used as a denial tactic, the five whys stops being a discovery tool and becomes a pretext — which also erodes trust with whoever is being asked the questions.

This unit doesn't argue for validating every request equally hard — it argues for matching the depth of investigation to what's actually at risk. A minor color tweak, low-cost and easily reversible, doesn't need the same process.

Treating every request identically either wastes time on trivial ones or under-invests in genuinely risky ones — proportionality is the actual discipline, not a fixed process applied uniformly.

Scrutiny should scale with stakes, not apply uniformly

This unit doesn't argue for validating every request equally hard — it argues for matching the depth of investigation to what's actually at risk. Bulk delete (destructive, hard to reverse, sets a precedent for how the team handles dangerous actions) earns a full five-whys treatment. A minor color tweak, low-cost and easily reversible, doesn't need the same process.

Treating every request identically either wastes time on trivial ones or under-invests in genuinely risky ones — proportionality is the actual discipline, not a fixed process applied uniformly.

Common mistake

Treating "always validate the problem first" as meaning "always run the full five-whys process," regardless of how small or reversible the request is.
